raw_case_text:
In October 2018, a 27-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of a pruritic rash on her face and ears. Her past medical history was significant for SLE diagnosed 5 years ago with cutaneous, joint, and renal tropism. She was treated with different treatments; first, she received 6 Cyclophosphamide boluses with relay by Azathioprine for 3 years, stopped for hematological toxicity, then switched to Mycophenolate Mofetil which was stopped by the patient herself for 1 year due to lack of means. She also had a notion of septic arthritis of the knee having recurred despite well-adapted antibiotic treatment and her aunt was being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis. Therefore, she was hospitalized this time to carry out the SLE systematization assessment and to update her treatment. In the initial physical examination, we found a malar rash; erythematous plaques on her face, ears, and upper limbs; and a diffuse non-scarring alopecia. She also had arthralgia especially in her left knee, with swelling in that area.
A small left knee effusion was aspirated and the culture was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis; therefore, anti-tuberculous therapy (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol) was initiated. The cutaneous symptomatology worsened after 15 days from the start of tuberculosis treatment with extended rash at the trunk and neckline, erythematous and edematous plaques, and blisters in the photo-exposed areas. Nikolsky's sign was positive, the affected skin surface was estimated to be 30%, and the mucosal involvement was limited to a simple cheilitis (Figure 1, Figure 2). The antituberculosis treatment was initially discontinued because we had thought of the TEN.
Laboratory abnormalities showed proteinuria elevated to 2g/24h, bicytopenia (leucopenia at 3500 per cubic milliliter and anemia with hemoglobin at 10 grams per dl), an elevated anti-double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) antibody with negative anti-histone antibodies and consumption of the complement C3 and C4. Moreover, skin biopsy showed diffuse epidermal necrosis, sub-epidermal detachment, interface dermatitis and presence of mucinosis. On direct immunofluorescence (DIF), a deposition of IgM and IgG in the basement membrane (lupus band) was present. Given the clinical history, lesion morphology, pathologic finding and laboratory studies, the diagnosis of TEN-like ACLE was established. After the administration of systemic corticosteroids, we have observed a healing of the skin lesions after two weeks. Anti-tuberculous treatment was reintroduced without any particular incident and Cyclophosphamide boluses were subsequently started. Joint swelling resolved within two months after the initiation of anti-tuberculous treatment and full joint range of motion was restored. There has been no recurrence of the bullous eruption to date.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presented in October 2018 with a 2-week history of a pruritic facial/auricular rash and painful left knee swelling, followed 15 days after starting anti-tuberculosis therapy by an extensive photo-distributed bullous eruption (30% BSA) with positive Nikolsky's sign.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year after self-discontinuing mycophenolate mofetil due to financial constraints, the patient presented with a malar/facial rash, diffuse alopecia, and recurrent left knee monoarthritis. Fifteen days after initiating HRZE for culture-positive left knee tuberculosis, she developed coalescing erythematous/edematous plaques and flaccid bullae over photo-exposed areas of the trunk, neckline, and limbs covering 30% BSA with simple cheilitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: SLE diagnosed 5 years prior (cutaneous, articular, and renal involvement; treated with 6 cyclophosphamide pulses, 3 years of azathioprine stopped for cytopenias, and mycophenolate stopped 1 year prior); prior recurrent left knee arthritis; household/family exposure to an aunt treated for pulmonary tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pruritic facial rash, alopecia, left knee pain/swelling, and subsequent bullous skin detachment.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam: malar rash, erythematous plaques on the face, ears, and upper limbs, diffuse non-scarring alopecia, and left knee effusion/swelling. Day 15 of ATT: erythematous edematous plaques and flaccid blisters on photo-exposed trunk, neckline, and limbs involving 30% body surface area with a positive Nikolsky's sign and simple cheilitis (without severe mucosal erosions).
objective.routine_investigations: 24-hour proteinuria 2 g/24h, leukopenia (WBC 3,500/mm^3), anemia (Hb 10 g/dL), elevated anti-dsDNA antibodies, negative anti-histone antibodies, and low complement C3 and C4.
objective.advanced_workup: Left knee synovial fluid aspirate culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Skin biopsy of the bullous eruption demonstrated full-thickness epidermal necrosis, subepidermal clefting, vacuolar interface dermatitis, dermal mucinosis, and a positive lupus band (granular IgG and IgM deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction) on direct immunofluorescence.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left knee joint fluid culture confirmed tuberculous monoarthritis, and skin biopsy histopathology with direct immunofluorescence (interface dermatitis, dermal mucin, positive lupus band, negative anti-histone antibodies) differentiated toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)-like acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (ACLE) from drug-induced TEN. Systemic corticosteroids healed the bullous lupus eruption within 2 weeks, allowing safe reintroduction of quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy (HRZE) alongside intravenous cyclophosphamide boluses, with complete resolution of left knee arthritis within 2 months and no recurrence of bullous lesions.
